content.summary:
## Overview

This section builds a fully scalable WordPress site (MyWordPress.com) that must serve picture uploads and keep user data and blog content in MySQL. It walks through the database layer (RDS Multi-AZ, then Aurora Multi-AZ with Read Replicas) and then the storage decision for uploaded images: an EBS volume attached to one instance versus EFS shared across the Auto Scaling group's instances in multiple Availability Zones. The exam tests this as the canonical "stateful app needs shared storage" scenario: recognise the EBS single-instance limitation and pick EFS for a distributed multi-AZ application.

## Core Concepts

- **Fully scalable WordPress architecture:** A WordPress deployment in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones, with content in MySQL and images on shared storage, so any instance can serve any user.
- **Stateful web application:** An application that keeps data or files on its instances (such as uploaded images), which conflicts with a stateless fleet behind Auto Scaling and a load balancer.
- **Auto Scaling group (multi-AZ):** The web tier: EC2 instances launched across Availability Zones 1, 2 and 3 that scale on demand and receive traffic from a load balancer.
- **RDS MySQL Multi-AZ layer:** The database layer for user data and blog content, deployed as RDS Multi-AZ so a standby in another AZ takes over if the primary fails.
- **RDS Multi-AZ:** A synchronous standby replica in a second Availability Zone, used for failover / high availability, not for scaling reads.
- **Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ:** Aurora keeps the same data in multiple AZs and provides easy Multi-AZ high availability without you managing replication.
- **Aurora Read Replicas:** Additional Aurora read endpoints that offload read traffic and improve read scaling; the section pairs them with Multi-AZ for scaling the database layer.
- **Storing images with EBS:** Images are written to an Amazon EBS volume attached to the instance; EBS is block storage tied to a single instance (and a single AZ).
- **EBS volume:** A block-storage volume attached to one EC2 instance; it exists in one Availability Zone and cannot be shared by instances in other AZs.
- **EBS single-instance limitation:** With an EBS volume, an image uploaded to instance A is invisible to instance B, so users hitting another instance in the Auto Scaling group see broken images.
- **EBS vs EFS for distributed apps:** EBS suits a single-instance application; EFS is a shared file system for distributed applications whose instances span AZs.
- **Storing images with EFS:** Uploaded images go to Amazon EFS, which is mounted by every instance, so any instance in any AZ can display any uploaded image.
- **EFS ENIs across AZs:** Each instance mounts EFS through an elastic network interface (ENI) in its own Availability Zone, giving all instances one shared file system.
- **Amazon EFS:** A managed, shared file system that multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones can mount at the same time — the fix for distributed upload storage.
- **Block storage vs file storage:** EBS provides block storage attached to one instance; EFS provides a shared network file system mounted by many instances, which is why EFS fits the distributed case.

## Key Comparisons

- **EBS vs EFS for uploaded images:** EBS is a block volume attached to one instance in one AZ, so other instances can't see the upload; EFS is a shared file system mounted by all instances across AZs.
- **EBS single-instance vs distributed Auto Scaling application:** If the app runs on one instance, EBS works; once an Auto Scaling group spreads instances across AZs, the images must live on EFS.
- **RDS MySQL Multi-AZ vs Aurora with Multi-AZ and Read Replicas:** RDS Multi-AZ gives a synchronous standby for failover only; Aurora adds easy Multi-AZ plus Read Replicas for read scaling.
- **Multi-AZ (RDS/Aurora) vs Read Replica:** Multi-AZ is for high availability / failover; Read Replicas are for offloading reads and read scaling.
- **Block storage (EBS) vs file storage (EFS):** Block storage attaches to a single instance; file storage is mountable by many instances simultaneously, which is what a distributed app needs.

## Common Misunderstandings

- EBS is not shared storage: an EBS volume cannot be mounted by instances in different Availability Zones, so it cannot back a multi-AZ Auto Scaling image upload.
- Multi-AZ is not for read scaling: the standby is for failover; read scaling needs Read Replicas (Aurora Read Replicas in this section).
- Adding more instances does not fix the image problem — without EFS, each new instance has its own EBS volume and misses previously uploaded images.
- EFS does not require all instances in one AZ: instances in different AZs each mount the shared file system through an ENI.

## Mental Models

- Think of EBS as a USB drive plugged into one server — only that server sees the file.
- Think of EFS as a shared network drive every server in every AZ can mount — uploads follow the user to any instance.
- Think of Multi-AZ as the spare tire (failover) and Read Replicas as extra lanes (read throughput).

## Exceptions & Edge Cases

- If the application is genuinely single-instance, EBS for images is acceptable; the problem appears only when Auto Scaling distributes instances across AZs.
- The database layer can be either RDS MySQL Multi-AZ or Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ with Read Replicas — the storage decision for images is independent of that choice.
- WordPress needs a writable shared location for uploads; EFS provides it for every instance behind the load balancer.

## When to Use Which

- Uploaded images must be visible to any EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple AZs → **Amazon EFS mounted by every instance**
- Application runs on a single EC2 instance and stores files locally → **Amazon EBS volume**
- MySQL database must survive an AZ failure → **RDS MySQL Multi-AZ or Aurora Multi-AZ**
- Database must also serve heavy read traffic → **Aurora with Read Replicas**
- Need a fully scalable WordPress site with user data, blog content and images → **ALB + Auto Scaling group across AZs + multi-AZ MySQL database + EFS for images**

## Patterns to Recognize

- "Users sometimes see broken or missing images after new instances launch" → **Images stored on EBS instead of a shared file system — move to EFS**
- "Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones storing user uploads" → **EFS is the expected answer; EBS is the distractor**
- "Database must be highly available and handle read-heavy traffic" → **Aurora Multi-AZ plus Read Replicas**
- "High availability with automatic failover to another AZ" → **Multi-AZ deployment, not read replicas**

## Exam Traps

- “"Use an EBS volume for uploads because it's attached to the instance and fast"” — EBS is single-instance and single-AZ; instances elsewhere in the Auto Scaling group cannot see those images. Use EFS for the distributed case.
- “"Multi-AZ RDS improves read performance"” — The Multi-AZ standby is for failover only; read scaling comes from Read Replicas.
- “"Attach the same EBS volume to instances in all AZs"” — That is the EFS pattern; EBS volumes cannot be shared across Availability Zones.
- “"Aurora Multi-AZ makes Read Replicas unnecessary for scaling reads"” — Multi-AZ addresses availability; Read Replicas address read scaling — the section uses both.

## Beyond the Source (tutor knowledge)

- EFS is a Regional, multi-AZ file system with mount targets per AZ; instances mount it over NFS through those targets.
- EBS volumes are AZ-scoped and replicated within that AZ; multi-attach io1/io2 volumes are limited to the same AZ and are not a substitute for EFS.
- Amazon S3 is a common alternative for WordPress media in a stateless design, but this section's comparison is EBS vs EFS.
keyPoints: EBS is attached to a single instance and lives in one Availability Zone — the canonical reason it fails for a multi-AZ Auto Scaling image-upload design.
EFS is the shared file system: every instance mounts it (each via an ENI in its own AZ), so any instance can serve any uploaded image.
The section's rule: EBS = single-instance application; EFS = distributed application.
RDS MySQL Multi-AZ provides a high-availability standby in a second AZ for failover — not a read-scaling mechanism.
Aurora gives Multi-AZ easily and adds Read Replicas — use it when the database must both survive AZ failure and scale reads.
The architecture spans an Auto Scaling group over Availability Zones 1, 2 and 3, an Elastic Load Balancer in front, and a multi-AZ database behind.
User data and blog content belong in the MySQL-compatible database (RDS MySQL or Aurora MySQL); images belong in EBS (single instance) or EFS (distributed).

quiz.question: A company runs WordPress on an Auto Scaling group spread across three Availability Zones behind a load balancer. Users report that images uploaded moments ago sometimes appear as broken images, and the problem gets worse as more instances launch. The database is unaffected. What is the most likely cause?
options: Images are stored on an EBS volume attached to each instance, so other instances cannot see them
Images are stored in Amazon EFS but the mount targets are only in one Availability Zone
The Multi-AZ RDS standby is not being used to serve image reads
The load balancer is not sticky enough to route each user to the instance holding their upload
quiz.explanation: EBS is block storage attached to a single instance in a single AZ, so an upload written on one instance is invisible to the others in the Auto Scaling group. EFS would be visible to all instances, so it is not the cause; the RDS standby is for failover and never serves image reads; stickiness would not help because new instances still lack previously uploaded files.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the difference between Amazon EBS and Amazon EFS in the context of uploaded images in a distributed application?
options: EBS is a shared file system; EFS is block storage attached to one instance
EBS is block storage attached to one instance; EFS is a file system many instances can mount
Both are AZ-scoped block volumes, but EFS allows multi-attach across AZs
Both are Regional file systems, but EBS has lower latency for uploads
quiz.explanation: EBS provides block storage attached to a single instance, while EFS is a shared network file system mountable by many instances. The reversed option swaps the two; EFS is not block storage and can be mounted across AZs; and EBS is not Regional nor a file system.
quiz.keyTopic: EBS vs EFS for distributed apps

quiz.question: A WordPress site runs on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones 1, 2 and 3, and user uploads must be readable by any instance. How should the images be stored?
options: On an EBS volume in Availability Zone 1 and shared with the other zones
On an EBS volume attached to each instance, synchronized between instances
On Amazon EFS, mounted by every instance in the Auto Scaling group
On the root EBS volume of the instance that receives the upload
quiz.explanation: EFS is the shared file system all instances across AZs can mount, so any instance can serve any upload. EBS volumes cannot be shared across Availability Zones; per-instance EBS with synchronization is not the section's design and does not provide shared storage; and a root volume is likewise single-instance.

quiz.question: How do EC2 instances in different Availability Zones mount the same Amazon EFS file system?
options: Each instance mounts it through an elastic network interface (ENI) in its own Availability Zone
Only the instance in Availability Zone 1 mounts it and the others copy the files over EBS
Instances attach the same EBS volume to reach the EFS mount point
All instances must be launched in a single Availability Zone to use one EFS file system
quiz.explanation: In the section's design every instance mounts EFS via an ENI located in its own Availability Zone, giving all instances one shared file system. EFS does not rely on a single mounting instance or on EBS volumes, and it does not require all instances to be in one AZ.

quiz.question: A single EC2 instance runs a small internal WordPress site with no Auto Scaling and stores uploaded images locally. What is the appropriate storage choice for those images?
options: Amazon EFS, because file storage is always preferred over block storage
Amazon EBS, because the application is single-instance
Amazon Aurora Read Replicas, because they offload image reads
An EBS volume replicated across three Availability Zones
quiz.explanation: The EBS single-instance limitation only matters once instances span AZs, so for a genuinely single-instance application an EBS volume is acceptable. EFS is unnecessary here; Read Replicas scale database reads and hold no image files; and a single EBS volume exists in one Availability Zone.

quiz.question: A WordPress deployment uses RDS MySQL Multi-AZ for user data and blog content. The team notices high read traffic on the database and asks whether the Multi-AZ standby can absorb it. What is the correct assessment?
options: Yes — the Multi-AZ standby serves read traffic, so no other change is needed
No — the Multi-AZ standby is for failover; read scaling needs Read Replicas or Aurora Read Replicas
Yes — but only if the standby is promoted first, which doubles cost
No — Multi-AZ must be disabled before any read traffic can be scaled
quiz.explanation: In RDS Multi-AZ the standby exists for failover / high availability, not read scaling. The standby does not serve reads; promotion is a failover action, not a scaling mechanism; and disabling Multi-AZ reduces availability rather than enabling read scaling.

quiz.question: A database layer must both survive an Availability Zone failure and handle a read-heavy WordPress workload with the least operational effort. Which design does this section recommend?
options: A single RDS MySQL instance with snapshots taken every hour
RDS MySQL Multi-AZ only, relying on the standby for read traffic
Amazon Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ with Read Replicas
Amazon EFS mounted by the database instances to share read load
quiz.explanation: Aurora provides easy Multi-AZ high availability and Read Replicas for read scaling, matching both requirements with minimal management. A single instance with snapshots is not highly available; RDS Multi-AZ alone gives failover but no read scaling; and EFS is file storage for uploaded images, not a database read-scaling mechanism.

quiz.question: A team proposes attaching the same EBS volume to every instance of a multi-AZ Auto Scaling group so all instances can read uploaded images. Why does this fail to meet the requirement?
options: EBS volumes can be attached to only one instance at a time and exist in a single Availability Zone
EBS volumes cannot store image files, only database files
EBS volumes are Regional and too slow for uploads from multiple AZs
EBS volumes require an EFS mount point before they can be attached
quiz.explanation: An EBS volume is AZ-scoped and attached to one instance, so it cannot be shared by instances in different Availability Zones — that is the EFS pattern. EBS can store any files including images; it is not Regional; and attaching an EFS mount point to an EBS volume is not a real configuration.

coreConcepts.definition: A WordPress deployment in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones, with content in MySQL and images on shared storage, so any instance can serve any user.
An application that keeps data or files on its instances (such as uploaded images), which conflicts with a stateless fleet behind Auto Scaling and a load balancer.
The web tier: EC2 instances launched across Availability Zones 1, 2 and 3 that scale on demand and receive traffic from a load balancer.
The database layer for user data and blog content, deployed as RDS Multi-AZ so a standby in another AZ takes over if the primary fails.
A synchronous standby replica in a second Availability Zone, used for failover / high availability, not for scaling reads.
Aurora keeps the same data in multiple AZs and provides easy Multi-AZ high availability without you managing replication.
Additional Aurora read endpoints that offload read traffic and improve read scaling; the section pairs them with Multi-AZ for scaling the database layer.
Images are written to an Amazon EBS volume attached to the instance; EBS is block storage tied to a single instance (and a single AZ).
A block-storage volume attached to one EC2 instance; it exists in one Availability Zone and cannot be shared by instances in other AZs.
With an EBS volume, an image uploaded to instance A is invisible to instance B, so users hitting another instance in the Auto Scaling group see broken images.

coreConcepts.term: EBS vs EFS for distributed apps
coreConcepts.definition: EBS suits a single-instance application; EFS is a shared file system for distributed applications whose instances span AZs.
Uploaded images go to Amazon EFS, which is mounted by every instance, so any instance in any AZ can display any uploaded image.
Each instance mounts EFS through an elastic network interface (ENI) in its own Availability Zone, giving all instances one shared file system.
A managed, shared file system that multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones can mount at the same time — the fix for distributed upload storage.
EBS provides block storage attached to one instance; EFS provides a shared network file system mounted by many instances, which is why EFS fits the distributed case.

mustRemember: EBS is attached to a single instance and lives in one Availability Zone — the canonical reason it fails for a multi-AZ Auto Scaling image-upload design.
EFS is the shared file system: every instance mounts it (each via an ENI in its own AZ), so any instance can serve any uploaded image.
The section's rule: EBS = single-instance application; EFS = distributed application.
RDS MySQL Multi-AZ provides a high-availability standby in a second AZ for failover — not a read-scaling mechanism.
Aurora gives Multi-AZ easily and adds Read Replicas — use it when the database must both survive AZ failure and scale reads.
The architecture spans an Auto Scaling group over Availability Zones 1, 2 and 3, an Elastic Load Balancer in front, and a multi-AZ database behind.
User data and blog content belong in the MySQL-compatible database (RDS MySQL or Aurora MySQL); images belong in EBS (single instance) or EFS (distributed).

keyComparisons.items: EBS vs EFS for uploaded images
keyComparisons.difference: EBS is a block volume attached to one instance in one AZ, so other instances can't see the upload; EFS is a shared file system mounted by all instances across AZs.

keyComparisons.items: EBS single-instance vs distributed Auto Scaling application
keyComparisons.difference: If the app runs on one instance, EBS works; once an Auto Scaling group spreads instances across AZs, the images must live on EFS.

keyComparisons.items: RDS MySQL Multi-AZ vs Aurora with Multi-AZ and Read Replicas
keyComparisons.difference: RDS Multi-AZ gives a synchronous standby for failover only; Aurora adds easy Multi-AZ plus Read Replicas for read scaling.
Multi-AZ is for high availability / failover; Read Replicas are for offloading reads and read scaling.
Block storage attaches to a single instance; file storage is mountable by many instances simultaneously, which is what a distributed app needs.

commonMisunderstandings: EBS is not shared storage: an EBS volume cannot be mounted by instances in different Availability Zones, so it cannot back a multi-AZ Auto Scaling image upload.
Multi-AZ is not for read scaling: the standby is for failover; read scaling needs Read Replicas (Aurora Read Replicas in this section).
Adding more instances does not fix the image problem — without EFS, each new instance has its own EBS volume and misses previously uploaded images.
EFS does not require all instances in one AZ: instances in different AZs each mount the shared file system through an ENI.
mentalModels: Think of EBS as a USB drive plugged into one server — only that server sees the file.
Think of EFS as a shared network drive every server in every AZ can mount — uploads follow the user to any instance.
Think of Multi-AZ as the spare tire (failover) and Read Replicas as extra lanes (read throughput).
edgeCases: If the application is genuinely single-instance, EBS for images is acceptable; the problem appears only when Auto Scaling distributes instances across AZs.
The database layer can be either RDS MySQL Multi-AZ or Aurora MySQL Multi-AZ with Read Replicas — the storage decision for images is independent of that choice.
WordPress needs a writable shared location for uploads; EFS provides it for every instance behind the load balancer.

whenToUse.situation: Uploaded images must be visible to any EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group spanning multiple AZs
whenToUse.use: Amazon EFS mounted by every instance

whenToUse.situation: Application runs on a single EC2 instance and stores files locally
MySQL database must survive an AZ failure
whenToUse.use: RDS MySQL Multi-AZ or Aurora Multi-AZ

whenToUse.situation: Database must also serve heavy read traffic
Need a fully scalable WordPress site with user data, blog content and images
whenToUse.use: ALB + Auto Scaling group across AZs + multi-AZ MySQL database + EFS for images

patternsToRecognize.signal: "Users sometimes see broken or missing images after new instances launch"
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Images stored on EBS instead of a shared file system — move to EFS

patternsToRecognize.signal: "Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones storing user uploads"
patternsToRecognize.indicates: EFS is the expected answer; EBS is the distractor

patternsToRecognize.signal: "Database must be highly available and handle read-heavy traffic"
"High availability with automatic failover to another AZ"

examTraps.trap: "Use an EBS volume for uploads because it's attached to the instance and fast"
examTraps.correction: EBS is single-instance and single-AZ; instances elsewhere in the Auto Scaling group cannot see those images. Use EFS for the distributed case.
The Multi-AZ standby is for failover only; read scaling comes from Read Replicas.

examTraps.trap: "Attach the same EBS volume to instances in all AZs"
examTraps.correction: That is the EFS pattern; EBS volumes cannot be shared across Availability Zones.

examTraps.trap: "Aurora Multi-AZ makes Read Replicas unnecessary for scaling reads"
examTraps.correction: Multi-AZ addresses availability; Read Replicas address read scaling — the section uses both.

beyondSource: EFS is a Regional, multi-AZ file system with mount targets per AZ; instances mount it over NFS through those targets.
EBS volumes are AZ-scoped and replicated within that AZ; multi-attach io1/io2 volumes are limited to the same AZ and are not a substitute for EFS.
Amazon S3 is a common alternative for WordPress media in a stateless design, but this section's comparison is EBS vs EFS.

sections.title: Instantiating Applications Quickly and the Typical 3-Tier Web App
sections.objective: Select the fastest way to instantiate EC2, RDS and EBS resources (Golden AMI, User Data, snapshots) and describe the standard 3-tier architecture with public, private and data subnets.
keyTopics: Golden AMI plus User Data hybrid
sections.text:
[Page 259]
Instantiating Applications quickly
• 	When launching a full stack (EC2, EBS, RDS), it can take time to:
• 	Install applications
• 	Insert initial (or recovery) data
• 	Configure everything
• 	Launch the application
• 	We can take advantage of the cloud to speed that up!

[Page 260]
Instantiating Applications quickly
• 	EC2 Instances:
• 	Use a Golden AMI: Install your applications, OS dependencies etc.. beforehand
and launch your EC2 instance from the Golden AMI
• 	Bootstrap using User Data: For dynamic configuration, use User Data scripts
• 	Hybrid: mix Golden AMI and User Data (Elastic Beanstalk)
• 	RDS Databases:
• 	Restore from a snapshot: the database will have schemas and data ready!
• 	EBS Volumes:
• 	Restore from a snapshot: the disk will already be formatted and have data!

sections.title: Elastic Beanstalk — Overview, Components, Platforms and Deployment Modes
sections.objective: Explain what Elastic Beanstalk manages versus what the developer owns, and distinguish web server tier, worker tier, and single instance versus load-balanced deployment modes.
keyTopics: Web server tier vs worker tier
Single instance vs HA deployment mode
sections.text:
[Page 262]
Developer problems on AWS
• 	Managing infrastructure
• 	Deploying Code
• 	Configuring all the databases, load balancers, etc
• 	Scaling concerns
• 	Most web apps have the same architecture (ALB + ASG)
• 	All the developers want is for their code to run!
• 	Possibly, consistently across different applications and environments

[Page 263]
Elastic Beanstalk 	– 	Overview
• 	Elastic Beanstalk is a developer centric view of deploying an application
on AWS
• 	It uses all the component’s we’ve seen before: EC2, ASG, ELB, RDS, …
• 	Managed service
• 	Automatically handles capacity provisioning, load balancing, scaling, application
health monitoring, instance configuration, …
• 	Just the application code is the responsibility of the developer
• 	We still have full control over the configuration
• 	Beanstalk is free but you pay for the underlying instances

[Page 264]
Elastic Beanstalk 	– 	Components
• 	Application: collection of Elastic Beanstalk components (environments,
versions, configurations, …)
• 	Application Version: an iteration of your application code
• 	Environment
• 	Collection of AWS resources running an application version (only one application
version at a time)
• 	Tiers: Web Server Environment Tier & Worker Environment Tier
• 	You can create multiple environments (dev, test, prod, …)
